## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Linemen and line inspectors who patrol a utility's poles.
   [HN] "Most utilities solve this problem with foot patrols. Linemen drive out with a clipboard or an iPad, and run
   through a checklist with binoculars to visually confirm everything is in order." [HN] "We're making weatherized,
   hybrid-fixed drones deployed for power utility inspections." → `roles[lineman]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Confirm every pole and line is sound before it fails.
   [HN] "But when the wood starts to rot, or the cotter pin falls out, and a live conductor is dropped on a dead tree on
   a windy day, you get devastating wildfires like the Palisades Fire in LA last year." → `context.job`,
   `statements.problem`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** On an inspection patrol, pole by pole from the ground; and reactive patrols after storms or a
   strange feeder reading.
   [HN] "A lineman can inspect about 50-150 poles per day, yet even the smallest rural electric cooperatives (with about
   ~20 employees) have about 50,000 distribution poles. Clearly the math doesn't work out. As a result, a given utility
   pole is inspected about every 10 years". [HN] "If there's a weird harmonic on a feeder, or a utility needs a rapid
   scan after a storm, we can get on-site within minutes to inspect." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: pole
   inspection patrol`. Author's choice: the window {3, MONTHS} (the research's "monthly cycle" rhythm; spec 120 reads a
   monthly rhythm as 3 MONTHS), Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most": not every lineman is put
   on patrols in a quarter; storm and construction crews may not be).

4. **Which people.** Linemen and inspectors at US electric utilities and rural co-ops.
   [HN] "The U.S. has 7M miles of power lines (enough to go to the moon and back 14 times), and they're aging." [HN]
   "Power utilities are our first customers". → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The utility, per pole or tower inspected.
   [HN] "Our business model is straightforward: inspection as a service. We charge per pole or tower." [HN] "We just
   secured our first major contract and are working out the details of pilots with some big utilities. Our first paid
   flight is mid-April." [LYC1] "If you're interested in piloting our service, reach out to avi@voltairlabs.com" →
   `persona.decision_maker: {role: manager}`. Author's choice: the decider is the utility's inspection manager and the
   tested role "The VP of operations" (with "The co-op board" listed): no public source names a buyer title. Purchase
   friction's tested item "An FAA waiver to fly beyond sight" is from [HN] (avigotskind, a founder): "There's no real
   way around BVLOS regs right now. The real problem is BVLOS + need to recharge." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444564 ;
   the pad safety review is from [HN] "The risk of landing a drone multiple times per day at myriad points around the
   network felt too risky for utility engineers."; the competitive bid is the author's. Commitment's step "pay for a
   pilot on one feeder": [HN] "Our first paid flight is mid-April"; "on one feeder" is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Fixed-wing drones that live outside and recharge on pads along the lines.
   [HN] "We're making weatherized, long-range (well over 70 miles), fixed-wing drones that can live outside for months
   at a time. They recharge inductively (no connections or moving parts) on stripped-down charging pads that cost a
   couple thousand dollars apiece." [HN] "we use the charging station as an intermediary, dumping the data from our
   drone to a hard drive on the station over a high-speed WiFi link." [HN] (wweissbluth, a founder) "We're collecting
   61MP RGB, LiDAR (DSM DTM) and radiometric thermal for sensors" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444631 .
   The earlier idea, dropped before the HN post: [LYC1] "We build drones that charge directly on transmission lines."
   and [HN] "There's not enough current on distribution lines!" → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`.
   Compatibility (pole tops visible from above — tested; a spot for a pad; findings into the work order system) and
   Adoption friction (review the drone's flags before sending crews — tested; work from a defect list) are the
   author's, from the mechanism's needs. Relative advantage: [HN] "Xcel power found drones to find 60% more defects than
   foot patrols (because of pole-top vantage point)" (less_worry) and the 50-150 poles a day (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.**
   Price: **the operator's reading.** [HN] gives the unit only ("We charge per pole or tower"); no amount appears in any
   launch-era or later source. The founder's price is set at **$3 to $5 per pole, each**, below the author's estimate
   of the foot patrol's cost per pole, since the founders sell on cost ([HN] "Georgia Power saved 60% on operating
   expenses when they switched to using drones"). Under the engine's `compare` reading the founder's ratio is 30% to
   125% of the cost (CommercialChain.derive).
   Cost, MONEY **$4 to $10 of the pole inspections per pole, each**: author's arithmetic. A lineman's day of 8 hours at
   [BLS] "The median annual wage for electrical power-line installers and repairers was $95,320 in May 2025" ($45.83 an
   hour) is about $367; with a truck and fuel, about $500 a day; over [HN]'s 50-150 poles a day, $3.30 to $10 a pole,
   taken as $4 to $10. The helicopter ($25k a flight) and the drone-in-a-box ($250,000 a box) are left as the founders'
   comparisons in the statement, not folded into the per-pole cost.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (Uncle_Clark) "I work for a utility company and this is brilliant. One other issue that comes into play for
   inspections is right of way." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47446642 ; [HN] (lifis) "Why not just install
   cameras on the poles?" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47452396 ; [HN] (petargyurov, who builds analytics on
   drone and helicopter imagery) "This is a tough problem to solve and for a lot of operators ultimately comes down to
   cost." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444350 . No first-person lineman account exists in the sources.

## Status today

Widened in pitch, same buyer. [YCP] today reads "Autonomous Drones for Earth Observation", with power utilities "the
perfect first customer" ([LYC2] 2026-03-13: "Power utilities are the perfect first customer. ... Voltair can serve
existing multi-billion dollar data markets in road, rail and telecom inspection at 10x lower prices"). [SITE] still sells
utility inspection only ("Voltair | Autonomous Drone Inspection for Electric Utilities"), with charging moved to
"Ground infrastructure at utility substations", and offers a pilot slot. Price today: none public ([SITE], read
2026-10-22: no price or per-pole figure).

- **The cost per pole.** The founders give poles a day, not dollars; $4 to $10 is the author's arithmetic on [BLS].
- **Volumes.** How many poles a utility inspects a year is not asked by Keel (no volume question on `each`); the
  50,000-pole co-op is in the statement only.
- **A buyer title** and every Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment item beyond those quoted in item 5.
- **First-person lineman accounts.** None in the sources; the stories are scripted from the founders' post and the
  thread.
- **Which launch statement is "day one".** [LYC1] (2026-01-23) pitched power-line charging; the entry uses [HN]
  (2026-03-19), where that approach is dropped, as the idea the founders held at launch.

screens.why5: Nothing is reworded in meaning: these are my three conditions, and my pick of pole tops visible from above carries straight into the test.
screens.instead: Keep the list and the question, but write the belief as "For most linemen, the pole tops on their circuits can be seen from above, not hidden by trees", and use one wording for the bar: "Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say only sometimes, or no."

screens.why1: Right after settling how it fits the way linemen work today, it is obvious to ask what it does better than the foot patrol.
screens.why2: The question is plain on first reading, and 'walking the line' is how my trade talks about a patrol.
screens.why3: I sell on this exact comparison with foot patrols, so I can answer it straight from what I know: the 50-150 poles a day limit and Xcel's pole-top defect finding.
screens.why4: The free-text box with a 25-word limit has room for both my benefits, and 'Leave this out of the study' is a fitting escape.
screens.why5: The belief line keeps 'every pole checked without walking the line' but drops 'defects on the pole tops seen up close', which is half of what I typed and the Xcel advantage I lean on.
screens.instead: Same question, with the belief carrying both benefits: 'For most, their last inspection would have gone better with it: every pole checked without walking the line, and defects on the pole tops seen up close.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, Keel shows me the benefit list drafted from that for me to check, so it is obvious why this screen is here.
screens.why2: Walking the line, pole tops and defects are everyday words in my trade, and the intro and the bar read clearly the first time.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my drones do better than a foot patrol, from the poles-per-day math to Xcel's finding of 60% more defects from the pole-top vantage point.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in my words, but the list has no row for the time saved on a patrol, the 50-150 poles a day limit, which is half of what I sell.
screens.why5: The meaning holds, but "without walking the line" drifts from my foot patrols, where linemen mostly drive out and check with binoculars, and the test belief carries only the first benefit while the intro says all are equal.
screens.instead: What it does better than today's way (reword, remove or add): Every pole checked, not just the few a patrol reaches / Pole-top defects seen from above / The circuit finished in far less time.

screens.why1: After fit and advantage, it is the obvious last solution question for me to ask what a lineman has to change to start using the drone's output.
screens.why2: The question and hint are short and clear, and from the earlier screens I know 'they' means the linemen and inspectors.
screens.why3: I built this service around how crews would work from drone findings, so I can answer from what I know, even before our first paid flight.
screens.why4: The box lets me say the change in my own words, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right escape if I don't want to test it.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my first step, reviewing flagged poles before sending crews, but it drops 'work from a defect list instead of patrolling' and adds a 'Most would' I did not type.
screens.instead: What will linemen have to do to start using it? Show both beliefs: 'Review the poles a drone flags before sending crews' and 'Work from a defect list instead of patrolling'.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'll have to do to start using it, Keel shows me its draft of those steps to check and pick from, so it is obvious why this is here.
screens.why2: Flagged poles, crews, a defect list and patrolling are how my customers and I talk, and the instruction to reword, remove or add is clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know what changes for a lineman when drones do the first pass: they review flags and work from a defect list rather than walking the circuit.
screens.why4: The two rows are in the trade's words and neither is nonsense, but they overlap as two sides of one change, reviewing flags and then working the resulting list, though I can still add a row if one is missing.
screens.why5: Both rows and the belief keep what I gave Keel, with the drone flagging and the crew acting, and nothing has drifted from my idea.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the two adoption efforts Keel wrote, it makes sense to choose the one that goes to strangers, and this is the last of the four solution beliefs.
screens.why3: I know how my service lands on a utility's crew, so I can judge whether reviewing flags or giving up patrols is the bigger hurdle.
screens.why4: Both efforts are real and distinct and in lineman words, but the belief picked, reviewing flags, is mild next to the unlisted hurdle of trusting the drone enough to stop walking the line, which the second option only half carries.
screens.why5: Both options and the belief keep what I confirmed on the previous screen, and the wording is unchanged as the intro promises.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, this is the obvious moment to decide whether to ask respondents for a next step, and I am already working out the details of pilots with utilities.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is my everyday word and the hint explains the mechanics clearly, but the bare "Offer a pilot?" doesn't say what is being offered until I read the hint, and "Pilot tab" is a Keel term I haven't seen yet.
screens.why3: I know whether I want pilot leads, and I am actively seeking pilots, so I can answer this at once from my own business.
screens.why4: Yes and no are complete and distinct for this decision, and both are worded plainly with no escape chip needed.
screens.why5: A pilot for me is a paid flight run on a utility's feeder and arranged with a manager, while "Would you try this for real? Leave your email" is a looser ask that, on my study, would mostly reach linemen who cannot sign one.
screens.instead: Ask people at the end if they'd try this for real? They leave an email, and you see who said yes on the Pilot tab. Options: Yes, ask them / No, don't ask

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, choosing who fronts the interviews is an obvious last setup step, and it follows naturally from the pilot offer.
screens.why2: "Linemans" is wrong (my trade says linemen, and I typed linemen who inspect poles), so it snags on first read, and the hint packs in video, voice, credits and text links, though the choice itself is simple.
screens.why3: I can listen to two five-second clips and pick the voice I think a lineman would talk to, which needs nothing beyond my own judgment.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with a sample each and a preselected default are complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape is needed because either one costs the same and the default stands.
screens.why5: My study is kept, but the plural I gave was "linemen" and the screen auto-pluralised my actor into "linemans", a small drift in my own trade's word.
screens.instead: Who should ask linemen your questions? Daphne (picked for you) or Saskia: tap to hear each. Recording the voice you pick costs 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, it is obvious why Keel asks how my linemen should answer.
screens.why2: "How should linemens answer?" is a plain question with a broken plural that makes me stop for a second, and "Hear her" and "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" run into the option text, though the choice itself is clear.
screens.why3: I know linemen work outdoors, in trucks and around noise, often on a phone, so I can judge whether they would rather talk or tap.
screens.why4: Talk to Daphne, read and tap, or let them pick covers the real choices, the three are distinct, and the readiness notes and loud-room claim are what I need to decide.
screens.why5: My trade's word is mangled to "linemens" ("linemen" is what I typed in the plural), though the meaning is otherwise kept and nothing else of mine is changed.
screens.instead: How should linemen answer? Options: AI interviewer (Daphne asks aloud on video; they talk, type or tap) / Read and tap (they read each question and tap; they can speak or type in any box) / Let them choose.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how linemen will answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before the study goes out.
screens.why2: I can answer it on first reading; 'a link', 'by name' and 'a group' are plain, and the Contacts page is explained well enough by its description.
screens.why3: I know whether I have named linemen and utility contacts to send to or would need to find or post to them, so this is my own decision to make.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real routes of named people, a searched list and an open post such as a lineman forum, and my true answer is there.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is kept as typed, and nothing on the screen changes what my study means.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly beside the deciding number, 4 answered with 5 needed, and it agrees with all three cards.
screens.why_b2: The page draws no chart, but the tally and cards show the count and the bar of 5; I need a second look to see why 7 people answered yet each card has only 4.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction and their belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, even though the statement above them is garbled.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' hints that I need more answers, but the page does not say how to get them, why 3 of the 7 did not count on any card, or what this means for the drones.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim about my belief from 4 answers, says plainly that the number is too few, and keeps both the 4 and the 7 visible.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 7 people answered, but only 4 could be counted on each belief (say why the other 3 were not) and 5 are needed, so get at least 1 more lineman who has done a pole inspection in the last 3 months before changing the drone plan; and fix the garbled sentence under the title so it reads as my solution.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside its deciding number, 4 answered with 5 needed, and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: The answer counts and the 4 counted are plain, but "your bar · 3 of 4 (no more than 1 in 3 say only sometimes or no)" took me a second look because it mixes the score, the marker and the bar's rule, and it never says one more against would break the bar.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "For most linemen, the pole tops could be seen from above" are what I checked on the way in, and the bar line repeats that belief.
screens.why_b4: It tells me nothing is settled and names Travis's no as the one to follow up, and his quote about thick timber shows me the concrete risk to check for my drones on lines under trees.
screens.why_b5: It shows 5 answered and 4 counted, explains why Dale is left out, calls this "a lean, not a call", and claims nothing beyond these people even though 3 of 4 looks good.
screens.instead: Say "3 of the 4 counted are for you, 1 against; your bar allows no more than 1 in 3 against. You need one more counted answer to call it, and Travis's line under timber is the case to check."

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is clear and the So line ties it to 4 counted of 5 needed, but the headline's '4 answered · 5 needed' contradicts the '5 answered' below it and the five names listed, so I have to read down to see why five people didn't meet a need of five.
screens.why_b2: Better 3 against Same 1 over 4 people reads at once, but the bar needs a second look because 'your bar · 3 of 4' sits beside 'no more than 1 in 3', and I have to work out that 3 of 4 clears it.
screens.why_b3: The name Relative advantage and the belief line are word for word the ones I checked on the way in, including 'every pole checked without walking the line'.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is honest and implies I need one more counted answer, but it doesn't tell me to get one or what the 3-to-1 lean means for selling drones to utilities.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the people who answered: n is visible, Dale's guess is excluded and named, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and the answer is flagged as hypothetical.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 linemen answered but Dale's was a guess, so 4 counted and 5 are needed; 3 of the 4 say a lot better, which leans your way, so get one more lineman's real answer before you lean on it.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits at the top, and "4 counted, 5 needed" gives the exact number that decides it, so I know why there is no call.
screens.why_b2: The answer counts per option and the for/against strip are clear, but "your bar · 3 of 4 (no more than 1 in 3...)" reads like both my result and the bar, so I need a second look to see that the bar is about the against share.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and "Most would review the poles a drone flags before sending crews" are the words I checked on the way in, though "You said review the poles..." is a clipped fragment.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is honest but generic: it does not tell me to get one more usable answer from a lineman or what that answer would change.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the people who answered and says "a lean, not a call", but the header's "4 answered" contradicts the count line's "5 answered", and 3 of 4 beside "your bar" could look like a pass.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 linemen answered and 4 could be counted (3 would review the flags, 2 of them only on a condition; 1 probably would not), so get one more clear answer before relying on this, and ask Jorge and Travis what would make the review worth it.

screens.why_b1: Each box states the verdict, Too few to call, with the deciding number right beside it: 4 answered, 5 needed to call it.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Relative advantage carry the names and belief lines exactly as I checked them on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The 5 needed implies I need more answers, but the screen never says to get more linemen or what the timber and crew-shortage answers mean for the idea.
screens.why_b5: Nothing goes beyond the people who answered: the verdict is withheld at 4, each group shows 1 against and 1 asked, and each quote stands as one person's answer.
screens.why_b6: I typed neither of these: lines under thick timber show only treetops from the air, and one lineman says trouble calls and being a crew short run the week while patrols do get done, which questions whether patrols are the pain at all.
screens.instead: Under each too-few status, say: one more answer is needed to call this, so send the study to more linemen, and ask them about lines under timber and whether patrols are really what runs their week.

screens.why1: A screening question makes sense first, but it jumps straight to missed damage, and the next screen then asks about poles coming due for inspection, not the miss, so a yes leads somewhere else.
screens.why2: Pole damage and ground inspection are everyday words in my trade, so I get it on first read, though it doesn't say whose inspection missed it.
screens.why3: I walk poles and know what I've found, but I can't always tell if an earlier ground patrol missed something or the damage came after it, so I'd partly be guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the chips are off: 'one particular inspection' doesn't fit a question about finding missed damage, and a yes-or-no gate shouldn't carry two escapes.
screens.why5: The job is checking due poles from the ground, but this question assumes ground inspections miss things, which sounds like somebody's sales pitch against the way I work.
screens.why6: It's one short question ending in 'Yes or no', easy to hear once and answer, with no escape read out, as a gate should be.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you inspect poles on a circuit from the ground? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After being asked about damage a ground inspection missed, it makes sense to be shown an idea for inspecting the poles another way, and the kicker says that's what's coming.
screens.why2: I know poles, spans, feeders, LiDAR and thermal, but calling drones a 'pole-by-pole inspection record' threw me, and I'd have to hear 'hop pad to pad' and 'pads send data back' twice to picture how it works.
screens.why3: Patrolling poles, finding damage and going out to check after storms or odd feeder readings is my job, so I can judge this from what I do.
screens.why4: It's a card to read with no options to pick from.
screens.why5: The drones, pads and rapid scans all come through, but 'inspection record' undersells them, and the belief just repeats the charging pads instead of saying why anyone would want this.
screens.why6: It's a long card to take in on one hearing, 'photos, LiDAR and thermal' is a mouthful, and the charging pads come round twice, though there's no slash or parenthesis to trip over.
screens.instead: Imagine Voltair, drones that inspect every pole and span for you. They live outside along the lines, recharge on charging pads, and send back photos, LiDAR and thermal; you can ask for a rapid scan after a storm or a strange feeder reading. The people building it believe this would find damage a ground inspection misses, before it fails.

screens.why1: They just showed me the idea, so asking whether it would have worked on my last inspection is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Fitted the way things were set up for you" is vague office talk, and I'd have to read it twice to work out whether it means our paper forms, the co-op's system, or how my patrol runs.
screens.why3: I know how my last patrol went with the clipboard and the checklist, but the card only says "a pole-by-pole inspection record," so I'd be partly guessing how it would sit alongside what the utility already has us fill out.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from easily to no without overlapping, and "I can't tell" is the honest out for someone who hasn't seen the thing.
screens.why5: Apart from the idea card shown on purpose, nothing of the founder's plan or terms reaches me, and it still asks whether the record fits how the inspection work gets done.
screens.why6: It's short and the options hold in my head, but "it" and "the way things were set up for you" are loose enough when heard once that I'd want it said again.
screens.instead: Think of your last inspection. Could a pole-by-pole record have fit how you write up your poles? Yes, easily; yes, most of the time; only sometimes; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after hearing the idea and whether it would have fit, it makes sense to ask if it would have actually helped on my last inspection.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and I'd know what it's asking the first time I heard it, the name Voltair having just been explained on the card.
screens.why3: I walk these poles with my clipboard and checklist, so I can say from my last patrol whether a pole-by-pole record would have changed anything.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover every answer I could give without overlapping, and I can't tell fits since all I've seen is one line about it.
screens.why5: The card shows the idea on purpose and the question adds no company talk or role labels, just my last inspection.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options I can hold in my head and one escape said last, so I could answer after hearing it once.

screens.why1: After being told about Voltair and asked if it fits and helps, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually do the one thing it needs from me.
screens.why2: I follow it on one hearing, but 'review the poles a drone flags' doesn't say what the review is, and whether I'd be the one sending crews is left loose, since a lineman usually gets sent rather than doing the sending.
screens.why3: I know pole damage and I've looked over pole photos and write-ups, but deciding which flagged poles get a crew is more my supervisor's or the engineer's call, so I'd be partly guessing.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from yes to no in words I'd use, and 'I can't tell' fits someone who has never worked from drone flags.
screens.why5: The drone step comes through as what I'd have to do, which is fair for an idea card, but 'sending crews' puts me in a dispatcher's or supervisor's role and drifts from the lineman checking poles from the ground.
screens.why6: It says well: two short sentences, one question, four short options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.instead: To use Voltair, you'd check the poles a drone flags before a crew goes out. Would you do that, or not? Yes; Yes, if it was clearly worth it; Probably not; No; or I can't tell.
